input: First-order reactions are extremely common in chemical kinetics, and the half-life is a particularly useful quantity because it provides an intuitive measure of how quickly a reaction proceeds. In this example, we are asked to determine the half-life of a first-order reaction with a rate constant of 0.046 min⁻¹ at 323 K, together with the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant itself was obtained experimentally from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a total period of 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life is related to the rate constant by the well-known expression $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$, while the fraction remaining after a time $t$ is given by $\exp(-k t)$. Substituting the measured value of the rate constant into the half-life expression gives $0.693 / 0.046 = 15.1$ min. Similarly, after 60 min the fraction remaining is $\exp(-0.046 \times 60)$, which works out to approximately 0.06. This result is consistent with the half-life, since 60 min corresponds to roughly four half-lives of 15.1 min each, and repeated halving rapidly reduces the remaining fraction. It is important to note, however, that these relations are valid only for a first-order reaction; a reaction of a different order would follow an entirely different decay law, highlighting the importance of establishing the reaction order before applying the formulas. The example also illustrates why the half-life is quoted so widely in practice when first-order behaviour has been established experimentally.
target:
Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction whose rate constant $k$ is 0.046 min⁻¹ at 323 K, and calculate the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life is fixed by the rate constant through $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ is $\exp(-k t)$. The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the starting concentration, because the rate falls in proportion to the concentration that remains: each equal time interval removes the same fraction of the reactant, not the same amount. Concentration measurements at regular intervals fix the rate constant because the logarithm of the concentration falls linearly with time for a first-order reaction. Substitution of the measured rate constant gives a half-life of $0.693 / 0.046 = 15.1$ min. The fraction remaining after 60 min is $\exp(-0.046 \times 60)$, which evaluates to 0.06. The stated half-life is a property of the reaction at the stated temperature: the rate constant, and with it the half-life, changes when the temperature changes, and the result is not carried to another temperature without a rate constant measured there.

The fraction can be checked against the half-life: 60 min spans about four half-lives of 15.1 min, and four successive halvings leave close to one sixteenth of the initial concentration, in agreement with the computed fraction. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life nor the fraction remaining can be obtained from the stated relations for such a reaction.
